newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo industry to grow slowly without foreign funds.
newsitem.headline: Yugo industry to grow slowly without foreign funds.

text.p: Yugoslavia will fall short of its official 10.8-percent industrial growth target for 1997, a Belgrade-based economic think-tank warned on Thursday.

"Scope for a more dynamic economic recovery has narrowed, with growth depending only on the country's ability to restore ties with international financial institutions," head of the Institute of Economic Sciences (IEN) Tomislav Popovic said.
Street protests for the past 53 days over local election fraud last November have rocked Serbia.

The United States have spearheaded a Western condemnation of Belgrade over what it sees was stomping of democracy and have indicated the possibility of restoring sanctions against Serbia unless opposition victory in elections in 15 biggest Serbian cities is respected.
Western economic experts and diplomats say many deals with Serbia have now been put on hold until the political crisis is resolved.
According to the official statistics, Yugoslav industry output grew 7.3 percent from January to November 1996.
But the economic situation is aggravated by the lack of capital and foreign investment, seen as crucial for Yugoslavia's economic recovery, IEN said in its latest report.
Announcing its 1997 industry growth forecasts, IEN presented three scenarios.
In the first one described as a status quo scenario, IEN saw industry growing seven percent.

It assumes nearly unchanged economic performance and trade gap financed through much of 1997 from unofficial hard currency reserves -- money held by Yugoslav banks and companies abroad. IEN expected those reserves to melt down by the end of 1997.
Another, probably more likely to happen, sees unofficial hard currency reserves exhausted by June 1997.

The country's trade gap will be curbed by the lack of those reserves and the only source to finance the trade gap will be surplus from the services sector, purchase of hard currency from citizens and remittances.
It also assumes Yugoslavia will have to start paying back interest on its foreign debt, probably to the extent of $500 million.
In this case, Yugoslav industry will either stagnate or grow by 2 percent, IEN economist Stojan Stamenkovic said.
The last, blackest scenario is based on expectations that Yugoslav creditors may activate the so-called cross default clause to collect payment.
Grace period for Yugoslav debt to commercial banks creditors signed in 1988, expired in 1994, Stamenkovic said.
Though unlikely to happen, Stamenkovic said it would mean a new sanction-like blockade of Yugoslav assets.
"But if it happens, the industry would slump by 10 or even 11 percent," Stamenkovic said. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
